summary: Michele Catasta presents Replit's approach to building coding agents for nontechnical users, framing full autonomy as the critical north star. He distinguishes supervised autonomy (Tesla FSD, requiring technical oversight) from full autonomy (Waymo, where users need no technical knowledge), pursuing the latter to let any knowledge worker create software. He identifies three pillars: frontier model capabilities, verification through autonomous testing, and context management. On verification, agents without testing create 'painted doors'—features that look done but are broken. Over 30% of agent-built features are broken initially. Replit adopted autonomous testing spanning static analysis, code execution, unit tests, API tests, and browser-based testing. For web applications, browser-based testing comes in two categories: computer use (one-to-one UI mapping via screenshots, expensive and slow) and browser use (simulated UI via DOM abstractions). Replit writes Playwright code directly, which LLMs handle well, is more expressive than generic tool-based approaches, and produces reusable regression tests—roughly an order of magnitude cheaper and faster than computer use. On context management, Catasta argues long-context models are unnecessary; most tasks fit within 200,000 tokens through proper context management: using the codebase for state, persisting plans on the file system, and dumping memories to files. Sub-agent orchestration is the key ingredient for long-running coherent tasks, analogous to separation of concerns in software engineering. Sub-agents start from a fresh context with minimal injected context, run to completion, and return only results. This reduced context recompression frequency from roughly 35 to 45-50 memories per compression in production. Testing was nearly mandatory to move into sub-agents because browser observations in the main loop confused the hedging loop. Finally, Catasta introduces parallelism as the next ingredient—not for making agents more powerful but for improving user experience. Sequential execution breaks flow; users write a prompt, leave for lunch, and hope it's done. Parallel agents trade extra compute for time but face problems: redundant context across parallel windows and merge conflicts that nontechnical users cannot resolve. Current user-orchestrated parallel approaches don't apply to Replit's user base. Replit's next agent version will use core-loop-orchestrated parallelism, where the core loop determines subtasks on the fly rather than the user. This removes the cognitive burden of task decomposition from nontechnical users and allows techniques from software engineering to mitigate merge conflicts, though corner cases will still arise. Catasta identifies this as Replit's main bet for the coming months and notes he is hiring.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and the Autonomy Landscape
sections.summary: Catasta introduces Replit's coding agent for nontechnical users and references the semiotic value plot showing the latency-autonomy tradeoff. He argues for a third dimension: building autonomous agents specifically for nontechnical users, distinguishing supervised autonomy (Tesla FSD) from full autonomy (Waymo) where users need no technical knowledge.

sections.title: Redefining Autonomy
sections.summary: Catasta argues autonomy should not be conflated with long runtimes or treated as a vanity metric. Tasks have irreducible complexity; the goal is maximizing reducible runtime—the span where users make no technical decisions. He introduces three pillars: frontier model capabilities, verification, and context management.

sections.title: Pillar: Verification and Autonomous Testing
sections.summary: Catasta details the verification pillar. Without testing, agents build 'painted doors'—features that look done but are broken. Over 30% of features are broken on first creation. Nontechnical users cannot provide technical feedback, creating a bottleneck. Replit adopted autonomous testing to break this bottleneck, prevent compounding errors, and overcome model laziness. He outlines a verification spectrum from static analysis through unit tests and API testing, noting each approach's limitations.

sections.title: Browser-Based Testing and Playwright
sections.summary: Catasta explains browser-based autonomous testing for web applications, contrasting computer use (one-to-one UI mapping via screenshots, expensive and slow) with browser use (DOM abstraction). Replit writes Playwright code directly, which LLMs handle well, is more expressive than generic tool-based approaches, and produces reusable regression tests—roughly an order of magnitude cheaper and faster than computer use.

sections.title: Pillar: Context Management and Sub-Agent Orchestration
sections.summary: Catasta argues long-context models are unnecessary; most tasks fit within 200,000 tokens through proper context management. State can be maintained via the codebase, file system persistence, and memory dumps. Sub-agent orchestration is the key ingredient for long-running coherent tasks, analogous to separation of concerns. Sub-agents start fresh, receive minimal context, run to completion, and return only results, reducing context recompression from ~35 to 45-50 memories per compression.

sections.title: Parallelism Introduction and Trade-offs
sections.summary: Catasta introduces parallelism as the next ingredient for improving user experience, not agent power. Sequential execution breaks flow—users write prompts and leave. Parallel agents trade compute for time but face redundant context (~80% shared) and merge conflicts nontechnical users cannot resolve. Current user-orchestrated parallel approaches don't apply to Replit. He previews a core-loop-orchestrated approach for the next agent version.

sections.title: Core-Loop-Orchestrated Parallelism and Closing
sections.summary: Catasta details the core-loop-orchestrated parallelism approach: the core loop, not the user, determines and decomposes subtasks on the fly. This removes the cognitive burden of task decomposition from nontechnical users and enables software engineering techniques to mitigate merge conflicts among parallel sub-agents, though corner cases will still occur. He identifies this as Replit's main bet for the coming months and notes he is hiring.
